title: Queen mate in a few moves
summary: King and queen against king: the box, the moment the queen stops, and the mate without stalemate.
part.box.title: The box and the two mates
part.box.summary: Where the mate happens and how the queen traps the black king without checks.
part.corner.title: Stop the queen, bring the king
part.corner.summary: Near the corner the queen waits, the king comes, and stalemate stays away.
step.t_seirawan: The black king is in the middle of the board, and our pieces are in the corner. What is the plan to take that king to mate?
step.t_seirawan.hint1: Mate only exists on the edge. Think about how the queen can take squares from the black king without giving check.
step.goal: You already gave this mate in the school. Now we give it well: fast, calm and without stalemate. I start from the end, because it helps to know where you are going. This is the first picture: the queen right next to the black king, on e7, protected by my king. The black king cannot take her and has no square to run to.
step.edge: The second picture: the kings face to face, mine on e6 and Black's on e8, and the queen checks from far away along the eighth rank. My king takes d7, e7 and f7; the queen takes the rest of the rank. Both mates only happen on the edge. So the plan has two parts: drive the black king to the edge and bring my king close to it.
step.jump: To push the black king, the queen does not need to give check. Put her a knight's jump away from the king, like here: king on e5, queen on f3. She becomes two walls, the f-file and the third rank, and the king is shut inside a rectangle. A check only pushes the king from one side to the other; a wall takes squares away for good.
step.follow: Your turn. The black king is in the centre and your king is far away. Use only the queen: after each of his moves, put the queen a knight's jump away again, so that the rectangle gets smaller.
step.follow.hint: Count the knight's jump from the black king and pick the square that shrinks his box. No checks.
step.follow.done: Good. Four queen moves, not a single check, and the black king has left the centre and is stuck in the corner. Other moves worked too, but the idea is always the same: follow the king like a shadow.
step.t_corner: The black king is in the corner and the queen is very close to it. Is this good for White? Count Black's moves.
step.t_corner.hint1: Look at each square next to the black king and who guards it. And check whether it is in check.
step.stop: Now the queen stops. The black king has only two squares, a7 and b8, and he will shuttle between them. If the queen keeps chasing him, she stalemates him. From here on the queen stays put, holding the box, and the one who works is my king, still on a1. This is the part that takes patience.
step.stalemate: Look at the danger. The black king is on a8 and the queen is on b6, a knight's jump away, just as I taught you. But now Black has no move at all and is not in check: stalemate, a draw. Near the corner the knight's jump is no longer the rule. Before every queen move, count the black king's squares: at least one must be left.
step.bring: The black king is stuck between g8 and h8, and the queen on e7 closes the seventh rank. Bring your king close and mate when it arrives.
step.bring.hint: The queen has done her job; leave her where she is. Walk your king up to the sixth rank, next to the black king.
step.bring.done: Mate. Notice that Qf6, on the last move, would have been stalemate: the black king with no square and no check. King close, queen protected, and only then the blow.
step.recap: Three rules to take with you. First: the queen a knight's jump from the black king, shrinking the box, no pointless checks. Second: when the black king has only two squares on the edge, the queen stops and the king comes. Third: before every queen move near the corner, count the black king's squares; zero squares and no check is a draw.
step.finish: Now play until mate, from the middle of the board. Box, edge, king, mate. And count the black king's squares before every queen move.
ex.e05: White to move. The black king is on the edge, but there is no mate yet. Make him walk into it.
ex.e05.hint: One queen move, no check, that leaves the black king a single square. After that the mate comes by itself.
ex.e05.solution: Qc7! closes the seventh rank and takes d8. The black king only has f8, and then comes Qf7#, protected by the king, or Qd8#, along the rank. Sometimes the strongest move is the one that threatens nothing: it forces the other side to move.
ex.e10: White to move and win. The black king is near the corner. Careful: there are two stalemates on the way.
ex.e10.hint: First, the queen a knight's jump away, leaving the black king a single square. Then the king comes, and the mate has several forms.
ex.e10.solution: Qe4! and the black king only has h3. Kf2 (Qg6 also works) and the king goes to h2. Now Qg2#, Qh4# or Qh7#. The traps: Qf4? on the second move, the knight's jump from h3, is stalemate; and so is Qf3? on the last one.
ex.e11: White to move and mate. Your king is not in front of the black king: it is a knight's jump away from it.
ex.e11.hint: The queen can stand right next to the black king if your king protects her. Look for the square touching him that your king reaches.
ex.e11.solution: Qd2#. The queen touches the black king and the king on c3 protects her; she takes c1, e1 and e2 herself, and the white king takes c2. Careful with Qe3? It is the knight's jump from d1, it takes every square without giving check, and the black king is stalemated.
ex.e12: White to move and mate. Again the kings are not face to face, and there are many checks on the board. Only one is mate.
ex.e12.hint: Your king already takes e2 and f2. You need a check from afar, along the first rank, that also watches the square left on the second.
ex.e12.solution: Qh1#. The queen checks along the first rank and, from the corner, also watches g2 on the diagonal; the king on e3 takes e2 and f2. Qf3+ or Qd1+ leave an escape, and Qg2+? gives the queen away. The edge mate does not need the kings in opposition: king and queen together just have to cover every square.
ex.e13: White to move and win. The queen already holds the black king on the first three ranks. What is faster: squeeze harder with the queen, or bring the king?
ex.e13.hint: The queen cannot mate alone. Think about which piece is missing to close the other side of the box.
ex.e13.solution: Ke2! The white king becomes the wall on the f-file: the black king only has g2, h2 and h3, and the queen comes in for the blow. The knight's jump Qe4 also holds, but costs two more moves, and sliding the queen along the fourth rank with Qf4+?, Qg4+? or Qh4+? gives her away. When the box is already small, the king does the work.
ex.e14: White to move and win. The black king is in the center and your pieces are in the corner. Only one queen move keeps the fastest path. Then keep going.
ex.e14.hint: There is more than one knight's jump. Pick the box that pushes the black king towards your king, not away from it.
ex.e14.solution: Qe7!, a knight's jump from d5: the walls are the e-file and the seventh rank, and the black king stays on the side of the board where your king is. Qe3, the other knight's jump, closes the box on the wrong side, far from the white king, and costs two moves; Qc5+? and Qd6+? give the queen away. After ...Kc6 the queen has done her part: Kb2 or Ka2, and the king comes.
ex.e15: White to move and win. The black king is close, but nothing is obvious: the fastest path has a single move almost every turn. Find them, and do not stalemate at the end.
ex.e15.hint: First, a queen wall that leaves your king on the inside, already near the black king. Then the king climbs right next to him, and the queen just waits.
ex.e15.solution: Qg4! closes the fourth rank and the g-file with your king inside the box (Qg5 also holds, but costs two moves; Qe3+? and Qd4+? give the queen away). After ...Ke3, Kc2! takes d2 and d3, and the black king must go to f2. Kd2 (or Kd3) and ...Kf1, then Ke3! steps up close, taking e2 and f2: ...Ke1 is forced, and Qg1# or Qe2# follows. The trap is on the fourth move: Qg3? takes every square without check and stalemates.
key.supportMate: The support mate: the queen right next to the black king, protected by the king. Diagram from Wikipedia (Checkmate article), after Pandolfini.
key.edgeMate: The edge mate: kings in opposition and the queen checks along the black king's rank. Diagram from Wikipedia (Checkmate article), after Pandolfini.
key.knightJump: The queen a knight's jump from the black king: two walls, no check, and the king shut in a rectangle.
key.cornerStalemate: The most common stalemate: king in the corner and the queen on c7, no check. Example from Wikipedia, after Fine and Benko.
key.seirawan: Seirawan's example, via Wikipedia: black king in the centre, queen and king in the corner. Closing the rectangle, the mate comes with time to spare.
key.lichessPractice: The Lichess Practice position (Piece Checkmates I, by arex): king and queen in the centre against the black king.
history: For centuries the piece beside the king was the ferz, which moved one square diagonally; with it, this mate was hard work. The queen got her modern move in Spain at the end of the fifteenth century: the Valencian poem Scachs d'amor, around 1475, already shows her that way, and the oldest surviving treatise to describe the new move is the book by Luis Ramírez de Lucena, the same Lucena who gives his name to this app and to a rook position. Since then, king and queen against king has been the first ending everyone learns, because it is the one that turns up most: every pawn that promotes leads to it. The classic books, such as Fine's revised by Benko and Müller and Lamprecht's, show that with best play the mate never takes more than ten moves, from any position. The real danger is not taking too long: it is stalemate.
practice: Now the real ending: king on c2, queen on c1, and the black king on d7. Box, edge, king and mate, without stalemate. Choose the time control and go.
